newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM says guards may have suspected defection.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM says guards may have suspected defection.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Thursday he suspects bodyguards of a defecting North Korean official knew of his escape plan.
Hashimoto said Hwang Jong-yop, a senior adviser to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, was surrounded by heavy security during a visit to Tokyo immediately before his defection in Beijing on Wednesday.
"Looking at video footage of Secretary Hwang's departure from Japan, it was clearly different from when he arrived," Hashimoto told reporters.
"On his departure, North Korean guards were tightly huddled two metres (yards) all around Hwang as if they knew he intended to defect," Hashimoto said.
South Korea says Hwang, one of 11 secretaries on the powerful secretariat of Pyongyang's ruling Workers' Party, was the highest-ranking Pyongyang official ever to seek asylum in South Korea.
The defection of Hwang, who was in Japan from January 30 until February 11 to attend an academic symposium, caught Japan by surprise, Hashimoto"s spokesman said.
"We had not anticipated such a defection at all," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told reporters.
Kajiyama expressed concern about possible adverse effects the defection could have on the situation on the Korean peninsula.

"We once had hopes for some progress in dialogue between South and North Korea after Pyongyang"s apology for the submarine incident, and I hope such prospects will not be diminished due to this," Kajiyama said.
Last year, a North Korean submarine made an incursion into South Korean waters, chilling always frosty ties between the two Koreas until Pyongyang apologised last month.
Asked if Japan expected political confusion in Pyongyang because of the defection, Hashimoto replied: "Naturally, it could be possible, but I have no idea."
